intro: Hi! In this lesson you'll learn to say how people do things: Budi drives carefully, the train goes fast, Bu Ani cooks really well. You'll also make words stronger or softer with very, really and quite. Warm-up: how do you speak English today: slowly, quickly or well?
teachingNotes: Core idea: an adjective (kata sifat) describes a person or thing (a careful driver, Budi is careful); an adverb of manner (kata keterangan cara) describes HOW someone does something (Budi drives carefully). Form: adjective + -ly (slow → slowly, careful → carefully with two l's, polite → politely). Spelling: consonant + y → -ily (easy → easily, happy → happily); -le → -ly (gentle → gently, simple → simply). Explain 'adverb', 'verb' (kata kerja) and 'object' (the thing or person after the verb, like English in 'speaks English') in plain words the first time.

Irregular adverbs to remember: fast, hard, early and late are the same as the adjective (a fast train / goes fast; works hard); good → well. No *fastly, *goodly. 'hardly' is a different word (= hampir tidak: He hardly sleeps); mention it as a warning, don't drill it. 'well' is also an adjective meaning healthy: 'I'm well' = I'm healthy / fine (the learner knows 'Very well, thank you' from greetings), so it doesn't break the 'after be use an adjective' rule. friendly, lovely, lonely end in -ly but are adjectives (a friendly waiter); there is no adverb form: say 'in a friendly way'.

The Indonesian trap: Indonesian uses one word for both jobs ('Budi hati-hati', 'Budi menyetir hati-hati'), sometimes with 'dengan' (dengan baik, dengan pelan). Common errors: *'He drives very good' → He drives very well; *'She speaks English fluent' → She speaks English fluently; *'She is carefully' → She is careful (after am/is/are use the adjective). Useful trick: if Indonesian can say 'dengan ...', English usually needs the adverb.

Position: the adverb goes after the verb, or after verb + object: She speaks English well, not *'She speaks well English' (never between the verb and its object). Some -ly adverbs can also go before the main verb (She carefully opens the box): accept it, but teach and test the end position. well, fast and hard never go before the verb.

Degree words: very, really and quite go before an adjective or adverb (very slowly, really good, quite well). Only really goes before a verb: I really like it, not *'I very like it' (Indonesian 'sangat suka' tempts learners to say 'very like'); 'very much' goes at the end (I like it very much). quite = cukup / lumayan: in British English 'quite good' is a little less than 'very good'; in American English quite is often as strong as very. 'quite a + adjective + noun' (quite a big house) is the usual order: explain only if asked. 'I quite like it' (British) is correct: accept it, but don't test quite before verbs.

Limits: use only present simple, present continuous, can and was/were (the chain is a1-adjectives). No past simple, no will, no going to, no comparatives or superlatives (more slowly, faster, the best). Don't teach link verbs (look, feel, sound + adjective) beyond am/is/are; if asked, say they take an adjective (You look tired). Adverbs of frequency (always, often) are already known; don't reteach them.

keyPoints.title: Adverbs with -ly, and the irregular ones
keyPoints.explanation: An adverb says how someone does something. Most adverbs are adjective + -ly: slow → slowly, careful → carefully. Spelling: easy → easily (y → i), gentle → gently (-le → -ly). Some are irregular and just have to be remembered: fast and hard don't change, and good becomes well. hardly is a different word (= almost not).

id.title: Adverb dengan -ly, dan yang tidak beraturan
id.explanation: Adverb (kata keterangan cara) menjelaskan bagaimana seseorang melakukan sesuatu. Kebanyakan adverb = kata sifat + -ly: slow → slowly, careful → carefully. Ejaan: easy → easily (y jadi i), gentle → gently (-le jadi -ly). Ada yang tidak beraturan dan harus dihafal: fast dan hard tidak berubah, dan good menjadi well. hardly adalah kata lain (= hampir tidak).

keyPoints.title: Adjective or adverb?
keyPoints.explanation: Describing a person or thing → adjective: a careful driver, Budi is careful (after am/is/are with no action verb, use the adjective). Saying how someone does something → adverb: Budi drives carefully. Indonesian uses the same word for both (hati-hati), so don't forget -ly. Put the adverb after the verb and the object: She speaks English well, not 'She speaks well English'.

examples.en: Bu Ani is a good cook. She cooks well.
examples.id: Bu Ani jago masak. Dia memasak dengan baik.
Dimas berbicara bahasa Mandarin dengan lancar.

id.title: Kata sifat atau adverb?
id.explanation: Menjelaskan orang atau benda → kata sifat: a careful driver, Budi is careful (setelah am/is/are tanpa kata kerja kegiatan, pakai kata sifat). Menjelaskan cara seseorang melakukan sesuatu → adverb: Budi drives carefully. Bahasa Indonesia memakai kata yang sama untuk keduanya (hati-hati), jadi jangan lupa -ly. Taruh adverb setelah kata kerja dan objeknya: She speaks English well, bukan 'She speaks well English'.

keyPoints.title: very, really and quite
keyPoints.explanation: very and really make a word stronger; quite makes it a little softer (= cukup, lumayan). They go before an adjective or an adverb: very slowly, really good, quite well. Before a verb, only really works: I really like it, not 'I very like it'.

id.title: very, really dan quite
id.explanation: very dan really membuat kata lebih kuat; quite membuatnya sedikit lebih lemah (= cukup, lumayan). Letaknya sebelum kata sifat atau adverb: very slowly, really good, quite well. Sebelum kata kerja, hanya really yang bisa: I really like it, bukan 'I very like it'.

assessment.rubric: Correct: The test / exam is quite easy. 'The test is very easy' = 30 (cukup = quite, not very). Missing is ('The test quite easy') = 40. 'quite easily' = 30 (after is use the adjective).

blocks.text:
You know **adjectives**: describing words for a person or a thing (*a slow bus, a careful driver*). An **adverb** describes **how** someone does something: The bus moves **slowly**. Budi drives **carefully**. It answers the question **How?**

Most adverbs are simply **adjective + -ly**: slow → **slowly**, quick → **quickly**, quiet → **quietly**, careful → **carefully**, bad → **badly**, clear → **clearly**, polite → **politely**. Indonesian usually keeps the same word (*pelan, hati-hati*), sometimes with *dengan* (*dengan pelan*). English changes the word.

id.text:
Kamu sudah kenal **kata sifat** (adjective): kata yang menjelaskan orang atau benda (*a slow bus* = bus yang lambat, *a careful driver* = pengemudi yang hati-hati). **Adverb** (kata keterangan cara) menjelaskan **bagaimana** seseorang melakukan sesuatu: The bus moves **slowly**. Budi drives **carefully**. Adverb menjawab pertanyaan **How?** (Bagaimana?)

Kebanyakan adverb cukup **kata sifat + -ly**: slow → **slowly**, quick → **quickly**, quiet → **quietly**, careful → **carefully**, bad → **badly**, clear → **clearly**, polite → **politely**. Bahasa Indonesia biasanya memakai kata yang sama (*pelan, hati-hati*), kadang dengan *dengan* (*dengan pelan*). Bahasa Inggris mengubah katanya.

blocks.text: Three spelling rules. **1.** Usually just add **-ly**, and keep every letter: careful → carefu**ll**y (the word already ends in l, so now there are two), polite → polit**e**ly. **2.** A consonant + **y** at the end: change y to **i**, then add -ly: easy → eas**ily**, happy → happ**ily**. **3.** Words ending in **-le**: change -le to **-ly**: gentle → gent**ly**, simple → simp**ly** (not 'gentlely').

id.text: Tiga aturan ejaan. **1.** Biasanya cukup tambah **-ly**, dan semua huruf tetap: careful → carefu**ll**y (katanya sudah berakhir dengan l, jadi sekarang ada dua), polite → polit**e**ly. **2.** Konsonan (huruf selain a, i, u, e, o) + **y** di akhir: ubah y jadi **i**, lalu tambah -ly: easy → eas**ily**, happy → happ**ily**. **3.** Kata yang berakhir **-le**: ubah -le jadi **-ly**: gentle → gent**ly**, simple → simp**ly** (bukan 'gentlely').

blocks.explain: simple ends in -le, so -le changes to -ly: simply.

id.explain: simple berakhir dengan -le, jadi -le berubah menjadi -ly: simply.

blocks.text: A few adverbs are **irregular**: they don't follow the -ly rule, so you just have to remember them. **fast, hard, early** and **late** are the **same word** as the adjective: *a fast train* → the train goes **fast**; *a hard worker* → she works **hard**. And **good** becomes **well**: *a good singer* → she sings **well**. There is no 'fastly' and no 'goodly'.

id.text: Ada beberapa adverb yang **tidak beraturan**: tidak mengikuti aturan -ly, jadi harus dihafal. **fast, hard, early** dan **late** adalah **kata yang sama** dengan kata sifatnya: *a fast train* (kereta yang cepat) → the train goes **fast** (keretanya melaju cepat); *a hard worker* (pekerja keras) → she works **hard** (dia bekerja keras). Lalu **good** menjadi **well**: *a good singer* (penyanyi yang bagus) → she sings **well** (dia bernyanyi dengan bagus). Tidak ada kata 'fastly' dan 'goodly'.

rows.en: The train to Bandung goes very fast.
rows.id: Kereta ke Bandung melaju sangat cepat.

rows.en: Pak Hasan works hard every day.
rows.id: Pak Hasan bekerja keras setiap hari.

rows.en: I sometimes get up late on Sundays.
rows.id: Kadang saya bangun siang di hari Minggu.

rows.en: Bu Ani cooks rendang really well.
rows.id: Bu Ani jago sekali memasak rendang.

blocks.text: **hardly** is not the adverb of hard. It's a different word that means **almost not** (*hampir tidak*): Pak Hasan works **hard** = he works a lot, but He **hardly** works = he almost doesn't work! So never add -ly to hard when you mean *keras*.

id.text: **hardly** bukan adverb dari hard. Itu kata lain yang artinya **hampir tidak**: Pak Hasan works **hard** = dia bekerja keras, tapi He **hardly** works = dia hampir tidak bekerja! Jadi jangan pernah menambah -ly pada hard kalau maksudmu *keras*.

blocks.text: Two things that look like broken rules. **friendly, lovely** and **lonely** end in -ly, but they are **adjectives**, not adverbs: a **friendly** waiter (pelayan yang ramah). They have no adverb, so say **in a friendly way**: *She talks to customers in a friendly way.* And **well** has a second job: it's also an adjective that means **healthy** (*sehat*). That's why How are you? — I'm **well**, thanks is correct after am: here well describes you, not an action. You know it already from *Very well, thank you*.

id.text: Dua hal yang kelihatannya melanggar aturan. **friendly, lovely** dan **lonely** berakhir dengan -ly, tapi ketiganya **kata sifat**, bukan adverb: a **friendly** waiter (pelayan yang ramah). Kata-kata ini tidak punya adverb, jadi bilang **in a friendly way** (dengan ramah): *She talks to customers in a friendly way.* Lalu **well** punya tugas kedua: well juga kata sifat yang artinya **sehat**. Karena itu How are you? — I'm **well**, thanks benar walaupun setelah am: di sini well menjelaskan kamu, bukan kegiatan. Kamu sudah kenal dari *Very well, thank you*.

blocks.explain: fast doesn't change: a fast runner, he runs fast. 'fastly' doesn't exist, and hardly means 'almost not'.

blocks.text:
Ask yourself one question: am I describing a **person or thing**, or **how someone does something**?
- A person or thing → **adjective**: Budi is a **careful** driver. After **am / is / are** (when there's no action verb) it's the adjective: Budi is **careful**.
- How someone does something → **adverb**: Budi drives **carefully**.

This is the Indonesian trap: Indonesian uses **one word** for both: *Budi hati-hati* and *Budi menyetir hati-hati*. English needs two different words. A trick: if you can say **dengan …** in Indonesian (*menyetir dengan hati-hati, berbicara dengan lancar*), English needs the adverb.

id.text:
Tanya dirimu satu hal: apakah aku menjelaskan **orang atau benda**, atau **cara seseorang melakukan sesuatu**?
- Orang atau benda → **kata sifat**: Budi is a **careful** driver. Setelah **am / is / are** (kalau tidak ada kata kerja kegiatan) pakai kata sifat: Budi is **careful**.
- Cara seseorang melakukan sesuatu → **adverb**: Budi drives **carefully**.

Inilah jebakan bahasa Indonesia: bahasa Indonesia memakai **satu kata** untuk keduanya: *Budi hati-hati* dan *Budi menyetir hati-hati*. Bahasa Inggris butuh dua kata yang berbeda. Triknya: kalau dalam bahasa Indonesia kamu bisa bilang **dengan …** (*menyetir dengan hati-hati, berbicara dengan lancar*), bahasa Inggris butuh adverb.

rows.id: Dia berbicara bahasa Inggris dengan sangat baik.

blocks.text: **Where does the adverb go?** After the verb (the action word): She sings **well**. If the verb has an **object** (the thing or person after the verb, like *English* in *speaks English*), the adverb comes **after the object**: She speaks English **well**. Never between the verb and the object: not 'She speaks well English'. Good news: Indonesian has the same order (*berbicara bahasa Inggris dengan baik*).

id.text: **Di mana letak adverb?** Setelah kata kerja (kata kegiatan): She sings **well**. Kalau kata kerjanya punya **objek** (benda atau orang setelah kata kerja, misalnya *English* di *speaks English*), adverb ada **setelah objek**: She speaks English **well**. Jangan di antara kata kerja dan objek: bukan 'She speaks well English'. Kabar baiknya: urutan bahasa Indonesia sama (*berbicara bahasa Inggris dengan baik*).

blocks.explain: It says how he plays, so it's the adverb well (not good), and it goes after the object (football).

id.explain: Kalimat ini menjelaskan cara dia bermain, jadi pakai adverb well (bukan good), dan letaknya setelah objek (football).

material.title: Stronger or softer: very, really, quite

blocks.text:
You know **very** and **really** with adjectives (*very hot*). They work with adverbs too: He drives **very** carefully. She sings **really** well. **quite** means **cukup / lumayan**: it makes the word a little softer. The food is **quite** good = lumayan enak, good but not very good. All three go **right before** the adjective or adverb.

Before a **verb**, only **really** works: I **really** like it, not 'I very like it'. The Indonesian trap: *sangat* is *very* in *sangat panas* (very hot), but *sangat suka* is **really like**, because *like* is a verb. You can also put **very much** at the end: *I like it very much.*

id.text:
Kamu sudah kenal **very** dan **really** dengan kata sifat (*very hot*). Keduanya juga bisa dipakai dengan adverb: He drives **very** carefully. She sings **really** well. **quite** artinya **cukup / lumayan**: membuat kata sedikit lebih lemah. The food is **quite** good = lumayan enak, enak tapi tidak sangat enak. Ketiganya ada **tepat sebelum** kata sifat atau adverb.

Sebelum **kata kerja**, hanya **really** yang bisa: I **really** like it, bukan 'I very like it'. Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: *sangat* = *very* di *sangat panas* (very hot), tapi *sangat suka* = **really like**, karena *like* adalah kata kerja. Kamu juga bisa menaruh **very much** di akhir: *I like it very much.*

rows.id: Tolong menyetir sangat pelan di sini.

rows.en: My little brother swims really well.
rows.id: Adik laki-laki saya berenang dengan sangat baik.

rows.en: My room is quite small, but it's clean.
rows.id: Kamar saya cukup kecil, tapi bersih.

blocks.text: **British vs American quite.** In British English, *quite good* is a little **less** than *very good* (lumayan). In American English, *quite* is often as strong as *very*. In this course, think **quite = cukup**. With a/an, quite usually comes **first**: It's **quite a** big house.

id.text: **quite versi Inggris Britania vs Amerika.** Dalam bahasa Inggris Britania, *quite good* sedikit **di bawah** *very good* (lumayan). Dalam bahasa Inggris Amerika, *quite* sering sama kuatnya dengan *very*. Di kursus ini, anggap saja **quite = cukup**. Kalau ada a/an, quite biasanya ada **di depan**: It's **quite a** big house. (Rumahnya cukup besar.)

blocks.explain: It says how he drives, so use the adverb well, and very goes right before it: very well. very can't go before a verb (drives).

id.explain: Kalimat ini menjelaskan cara dia menyetir, jadi pakai adverb well, dan very ada tepat sebelumnya: very well. very tidak bisa ada sebelum kata kerja (drives).

id.title: Lebih kuat atau lebih lemah: very, really, quite
